key_claims: Nearly half of dementia cases may be connected to risk factors that people can potentially change, including smoking and high blood pressure.

Most modifiable risk factors examined, including smoking, cardiovascular disease, high blood lipids, and high blood pressure, were linked to damage to the brain's blood vessels and faster accumulation of white matter changes.
Diabetes was associated with increased accumulation of amyloid β, while people with lower BMI had faster accumulation of tau, but these findings need further investigation.
Improving vascular and metabolic health may help reduce the combined effects of several brain changes that occur simultaneously.
limitations: The study involved almost 500 participants with an average age of 65 and no signs of cognitive impairment, which may not represent the general population.
The findings on diabetes and BMI are preliminary and need validation in future studies.
The source does not specify the exact proportion of dementia cases linked to modifiable risks, only that it is 'nearly half'.
The study duration was four years, which may not capture long-term effects.
what_not_to_say: The study proves that changing lifestyle habits can prevent dementia.
The study identifies all risk factors for dementia.
The study shows that smoking directly causes vascular dementia.
The study provides a specific percentage of dementia cases linked to modifiable risks.
The study recommends specific lifestyle changes for individuals.
